message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

The case for moving closer to the competitive set may be sound, but the proposal doesn't yet support it. It has a factual inconsistency that inflates the revenue figure, it reads its price-sensitivity evidence as stronger than it is, and the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's largest single source of Saturday demand. I'd send it back for revision rather than approve it as written.

## Major issues

**1. The room count is inconsistent, and the revenue figure uses the wrong one.**
Section 2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**. Section 5 calculates on **124 rooms**.
- 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£203,800**, which is the figure quoted.
- 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**.

If 112 is correct, the headline is overstated by about £20,000 (11%) before any other adjustment.

**2. The price-sensitivity evidence is confounded by seasonality.**
Section 3 credits the rise from 81% (June) to 89% (July) to the £10 rate increase. But Section 2 already says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. A June-to-July rise would be expected at any price.
- To isolate the price effect, compare July–December 2025 against the same months in 2024, or against the competitive set's movement over the same period.
- The claim that a higher rate "reinforced our positioning" has nothing behind it.

**3. The proposed increase is proportionally much larger than the one tested.**
The 2025 increase was £10 on £135, or **7.4%**. The proposed one is £20 on £145, or **13.8%**. Even if the earlier increase had been absorbed, that wouldn't show guests will absorb nearly twice the proportional rise. The new rate also removes Harbourside's price advantage entirely: £165 is the bottom of the competitors' range.

**4. The "value for money" score cuts the other way.**
Weekend guests rate value for money at 8.4/10, the highest in the set. That is most plausibly *because* Harbourside is £20–35 cheaper. It's a reason to expect this score, and possibly conversion, to fall after the increase. It is not evidence that guests won't notice it.

**5. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business.**
Section 4 says weddings at Quayside Hall make up about **38% of Saturday-night bookings**, and that these guests typically stay Saturday night only. A two-night minimum on Saturday stays would apply directly to them. The proposal doesn't address this. The hotel would have three options:
- Exempt wedding blocks, which undermines much of the policy's purpose.
- Enforce the minimum and risk losing wedding blocks, and possibly the venue relationship, to competitors.
- Make guests pay for a Friday or Sunday they don't want, which damages satisfaction and referrals.

Only already-contracted group rates are protected (Section 6). Future wedding blocks are not.

**6. On non-sold-out Saturdays, the minimum turns away demand.**
The hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays. On the other ~21, a single-night Saturday guest is incremental revenue. A minimum stay would turn some of them away. Even on sold-out nights, the gain depends on guests accepting the extra night rather than booking a competitor without a minimum. The claim that the minimum will "convert" stays assumes full compliance.

**7. The "prudent" assumption is the least prudent one available.**
Section 5 assumes zero occupancy loss from a 13.8% price rise *and* a new booking restriction. That is a best case. The recommendation then raises "about £204,000" to "**at least** £204,000", which the analysis doesn't support.

## Secondary issues

- **Not all weekend rooms sell at BAR.** Corporate rates, contracted group rates (including wedding blocks), OTA promotions and packages will not all move by £20. Applying the increase to every occupied weekend room overstates the gain even at 112 rooms.
- **The baseline mixes two rates.** January–June 2025 occupancy was achieved at £135, and July–December at £145. "Maintaining 2025 levels" is therefore partly a comparison with a cheaper rate.
- **The monitoring trigger is slow and loose.** The proposal reviews monthly and acts only if occupancy falls more than 5 points below 2025. A 5-point drop at 112 rooms is roughly 580 room-nights a year, worth about £96,000 at £165, before the trigger even fires. Weekly pick-up is already tracked, so a pace-based trigger would catch problems sooner. It should also track average length of stay and wedding block volumes.
- **The two-night minimum is unquantified** yet described as "material". At minimum, estimate how many single-night Saturday stays there were on sold-out nights, and how many Fridays and Sundays had spare rooms.
- **"Recovered strongly since 2023"** has no data behind it. The table covers only 2025.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the room count and recalculate. Apply the uplift only to the BAR-priced share of weekend room-nights.
2. Replace the June-to-July comparison with a year-on-year or comp-set-adjusted comparison.
3. Model at least two scenarios with occupancy loss, for example −3 and −6 points, and show the break-even occupancy. At £165 versus £145, revenue breaks even if occupancy falls by about 12% in relative terms, from 79% to about 69%. That headroom is a stronger argument than claiming no loss.
4. Separate the two proposals. The rate increase could go ahead. The minimum stay needs a decision on wedding guests, and could be restricted to peak Saturdays (for example, festival weekends) or applied through dynamic length-of-stay controls rather than a blanket rule.
5. Change "at least £204,000" to a range that reflects the scenarios.

**Note on timing:** the document is dated April 2026 for a 1 June start. If it was approved, there are now about five months of actual results. Weekend occupancy, average length of stay and wedding bookings for June–October 2026 compared with 2025 would test the proposal's assumptions far better than anything in it.
